{{Short description|Mathematical theory dealing with countable sets}}
{{Hatnote|Not to be confused with Tennenbaum's construction of a computable copy of <math>\omega + \omega^*</math> having no computable infinite ascending or descending chains.}}

'''Tennenbaum's theorem''', named for [[Stanley Tennenbaum]] who presented the theorem in 1959, is a result in [[mathematical logic]] that states that no [[countable set|countable]] [[Non-standard model of arithmetic|nonstandard model]] of [[first-order logic|first-order]] [[Peano arithmetic]] (PA) can be recursive.<ref>Kaye 1991, pp. 153ff.</ref>

==Recursive structures for PA==
A [[model theory|structure]] <math>M</math> in the language of PA is '''recursive''' if there are [[μ-recursive function|recursive]] functions <math>\oplus</math> and <math>\otimes</math> from <math> \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}</math> to <math>\mathbb{N}</math>, a recursive two-place relation <<sub>''M''</sub> on <math>\mathbb{N}</math>, and distinguished constants <math>n_0,n_1</math> such that
: <math>
(\mathbb{N}, \oplus,\otimes,<_M,n_{0},n_{1}) \cong M,
</math>
where <math>\cong</math> indicates [[isomorphism]] and <math>\mathbb{N}</math> is the set of (standard) [[natural numbers]]. Because the isomorphism must be a [[bijection]], every recursive model is countable. There are many nonisomorphic countable nonstandard models of PA.

Equivalently, <math>M</math> is recursive iff there exists a bijection <math>f: M \to \mathbb{N}</math>, such that the relationships <math>f(m) +_M f(n) = f(k)</math>, <math>f(m) \times_M f(n) = f(k)</math>, and <math>f(m) <_M f(n)</math> are computationally decidable.

== Statement of the theorem ==
Tennenbaum's theorem states that no countable nonstandard model of PA is recursive. Moreover, neither the addition nor the multiplication of such a model can be recursive.

== Proof sketch==

This sketch follows the argument presented by Kaye (1991). The first step in the proof is to show that, if ''M'' is any countable nonstandard model of PA, then the standard system of ''M'' (defined below) contains at least one nonrecursive set ''S''.  The second step is to show that, if either the addition or multiplication operation on ''M'' were recursive, then this set ''S'' would be recursive, which is a contradiction. 

Through the methods used to code ordered tuples, each element <math>x \in M</math> can be viewed as a code for a set <math>S_x</math> of elements of ''M''. In particular, if we let <math>p_i</math> be the ''i''th prime in ''M'', then <math>z \in S_x \leftrightarrow M \vDash p_z | x</math>.   Each set <math>S_x</math> will be bounded in ''M'', but if ''x'' is nonstandard then the set <math>S_x</math> may contain infinitely many standard natural numbers. The '''standard system''' of the model is the collection <math>\{ S_x \cap \mathbb{N} : x \in M\}</math>.   It can be shown that the standard system of any nonstandard model of PA contains a nonrecursive set, either by appealing to the [[incompleteness theorem]] or by directly considering a pair of [[Recursively inseparable sets|recursively inseparable]] r.e. sets.<ref>Kaye 1991, p. 154</ref> These are disjoint r.e. sets <math>A,B \subseteq \mathbb{N}</math> so that there is no recursive set <math>C \subseteq \mathbb{N}</math> with <math>A \subseteq C</math> and <math>B \cap C = \emptyset</math>. 

For the latter construction, begin with a pair of recursively inseparable r.e. sets ''A'' and ''B''.  For natural number ''x'' there is a ''y'' such that, for all ''i < x'', if <math>i \in A</math> then <math>p_i | y</math> and if <math>i \in B</math> then <math>p_i \nmid y</math>. By the [[overspill (arithmetic)|overspill]] property, this means that there is some nonstandard ''x'' in ''M'' for which there is a (necessarily nonstandard) ''y'' in ''M'' so that, for every <math>m \in M</math> with <math>m <_M x</math>, we have
:<math>M \vDash (m \in A\to p_m |y)\land(m\in B \to p_m \nmid y)</math>
Let <math>S = \mathbb{N} \cap S_y</math> be the corresponding set in the standard system of ''M''. Because ''A'' and ''B'' are r.e., one can show that <math>A \subseteq S</math> and <math>B \cap S = \emptyset</math>. Hence ''S'' is a separating set for ''A'' and ''B'', and by the choice of ''A'' and ''B'' this means ''S'' is nonrecursive. 

Now, to prove Tennenbaum's theorem, begin with a nonstandard countable model ''M'' and an element ''a'' in ''M'' so that <math>S = \mathbb{N} \cap S_a</math> is nonrecursive. The proof method shows that, because of the way the standard system is defined, it is possible to compute the characteristic function of the set ''S'' using the addition function <math>\oplus</math> of ''M'' as an oracle.  In particular, if <math>n_0</math> is the element of ''M'' corresponding to 0, and <math>n_1</math> is the element of ''M'' corresponding to 1, then for each <math>i \in \mathbb{N}</math> we can compute <math>n_i = n_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus n_1</math> (''i'' times).  To decide if a number ''n'' is in ''S'', first compute ''p'', the ''n''th prime in <math>\mathbb{N}</math>. Then, search for an element ''y'' of ''M'' so that 
:<math>a = \underbrace{y \oplus y \oplus \cdots \oplus y}_{p \text{ times}} \oplus n_i</math>
for some <math>i < p</math>. This search will halt because the [[Euclidean algorithm]] can be applied to any model of PA.  Finally, we have <math>n \in S</math> if and only if the ''i'' found in the search was 0. Because ''S'' is not recursive, this means that the addition operation on ''M'' is nonrecursive. 

A similar argument shows that it is possible to compute the characteristic function of ''S'' using the multiplication of ''M'' as an oracle, so the multiplication operation on ''M'' is also nonrecursive (Kaye&nbsp;1991:154).

== Turing degrees of models of PA ==

Jockush and Soare have shown there exists a model of PA with [[Low (computability)|low degree]].<ref>V. Harizanov, ''[https://home.gwu.edu/~harizanv/HandbookOriginalHarizanov.pdf Chapter 1: Pure Computable Model Theory]'', in ''Handbook of Recursive Mathematics'', edited by Yu. L. Ershov, S. S. Goncharov, A. Nerode, J. B. Remmel (1998, Elsevier). Chapter 1,  p.13</ref>
